options.A: Moral principles which govern a person's behaviour or conducting of an activity - a state of mind to act and perform in accordance with moral principles
options.B: A set of statutory penalties prescribed exclusively under the Companies Act, 2013

question_html: If management imposes a limitation on the scope of the auditor's work in the terms of a proposed audit engagement, such that the auditor believes it will result in disclaiming an opinion, the auditor shall:

options.A: Not accept such a limited engagement as an audit engagement, unless required by law or regulation to do so
options.B: Accept the engagement and issue a disclaimer of opinion at the conclusion of the audit without further discussion
options.C: Accept the engagement but limit the scope of the engagement letter to exclude reference to the limitation
options.D: Accept the engagement only if the client agrees to double the audit fee to compensate for the added risk

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Not accept such a limited engagement as an audit engagement, unless required by law or regulation to do so

If management or those charged with governance impose a limitation on the scope of the auditor's work in the terms of a proposed audit engagement such that the auditor believes the limitation will result in disclaiming an opinion, the auditor shall not accept such a limited engagement as an audit engagement, unless required by law or regulation to do so.

question_html: Management of an entity feels it unnecessary to give in writing that it understands its responsibility for preparation of financial statements in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework. What should the auditor do?

options.B: The auditor should not accept the proposed engagement, since this acknowledgment is a necessary precondition for an audit under SA 210, and the audit is conducted on the basic premise that management accepts this responsibility
options.A: The auditor may proceed with the audit without such acknowledgment, since it is merely a formality with no legal significance
options.C: The auditor should proceed but note the refusal only in the working papers, without any impact on engagement acceptance
options.D: The auditor should proceed and instead obtain an indemnity bond from the client's bankers

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The auditor should not accept the proposed engagement, since this acknowledgment is a necessary precondition for an audit under SA 210, and the audit is conducted on the basic premise that management accepts this responsibility

It is necessary for management to give in writing that it understands its responsibility for preparation of financial statements in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework, as this is a necessary precondition for an audit under SA 210; unless required by law or regulation, refusal by management on this point means the auditor should not accept the proposed engagement, since the audit is conducted on this basic premise.

question_html: As per SA 210, the auditor shall not agree to a change in the terms of the audit engagement:

options.C: Where there is no reasonable justification for doing so

question_html: Which of the following would generally NOT be considered a reasonable basis for a request to change the terms of the audit engagement?

options.D: A request to change the engagement to a review engagement in order to avoid a qualified opinion or a disclaimer of opinion, where the auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding a material item
options.A: A change in circumstances that affects the entity's requirements for the service
options.B: A misunderstanding as to the nature of an audit as originally requested by the entity
options.C: A restriction on the scope of the audit engagement caused by circumstances outside management's control

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) A request to change the engagement to a review engagement in order to avoid a qualified opinion or a disclaimer of opinion, where the auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding a material item

A change may not be considered reasonable if it appears that the change relates to information that is incorrect, incomplete or otherwise unsatisfactory - for example, where the auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding receivables and the entity asks for the engagement to be changed to a review engagement to avoid a qualified opinion or disclaimer.

options.B: Automatically accede to the request, since a lower level of assurance always represents a lower audit risk for the firm

options.D: Change the engagement without any documentation, since the change is presumed to be in the client's favour

The auditor shall determine whether there is reasonable justification for changing to a lower level of assurance engagement; if there is reasonable justification, the audit work performed to date may be relevant, but the report on the related service would ordinarily not include reference to the original audit engagement or procedures performed, except where changed to an agreed-upon procedures engagement.

options.C: An audit which is performed by an auditor over years

options.B: An audit conducted simultaneously by two independent audit firms for the same client
options.D: An audit limited exclusively to entities that have changed their auditor in the current year

A recurring audit is an audit which is performed by an auditor over years; on recurring audits, the auditor shall assess whether circumstances require the terms of the audit engagement to be revised, or whether there is a need to remind the entity of the existing terms.

question_html: Which of the following is identified as a factor that may make it appropriate to revise the terms of the audit engagement, or remind the entity of existing terms, in a recurring audit?

options.D: A significant change in the nature or size of the entity's business, or a recent change of senior management
options.A: The auditor having completed the audit ahead of the agreed timeline in the preceding year
options.B: The client having paid the audit fee promptly in the preceding year
options.C: The engagement partner having been with the firm for more than ten years

answer_html:

Factors that may make it appropriate to revise the terms of the audit engagement, or remind the entity of existing terms, include: any indication that the entity misunderstands the objective/scope of the audit, any revised or special terms, a recent change of senior management, a significant change in ownership, a significant change in nature or size of the entity's business, a change in legal/regulatory requirements, a change in the financial reporting framework, or a change in other reporting requirements.

options.B: Yes, a new engagement letter is mandatorily required to be issued before commencement of every recurring audit, without exception

question_html: The purpose of an independent audit, in relation to audit quality, is:

options.B: To provide confidence to users of audited financial statements, making high audit quality essential to maintain confidence in the independent assurance provided by auditors, with the auditor responsible for maintaining that quality
options.A: To provide an absolute guarantee that no fraud whatsoever has occurred in the entity's financial statements
options.C: To reduce the audit fee payable by the client through efficiencies in engagement performance

The purpose of an independent audit is to provide confidence to users of audited financial statements; therefore, high audit quality is essential to maintain confidence in the independent assurance provided by auditors, and it is the responsibility of the auditor to maintain high audit quality.

options.A: SQC 1 applies only to a particular audit engagement, while SA 220 applies to the entire firm across all engagement types

Self-review threats occur when, during a review of any judgement or conclusion reached in a previous audit or non-audit engagement, the auditor evaluates work that the firm itself performed; here, CA Devraj evaluating the effectiveness of the inventory module his firm designed is a classic self-review threat.

case_facts_html: CA Tanish Bhalerao, in the course of three separate engagements, encounters the following situations. Situation 1: While preparing a valuation certificate for a client's machinery to help the client save on certain regulatory fees, he knowingly certifies a cost figure that is significantly lower than the figure recorded in the client's own asset register, without any basis for the discrepancy. Situation 2: While conducting a statutory audit, he identifies a complex revenue recognition issue involving a recently issued Ind AS amendment, but does not update his knowledge of the amendment before forming his opinion, despite the amendment being directly relevant to a material transaction. Situation 3: CA Bhalerao is asked to audit the accounts of a partnership firm in which his own brother is a partner holding a substantial capital contribution.
question_html: Which fundamental principle does CA Bhalerao violate in Situation 1, by knowingly certifying a materially incorrect cost figure?

options.B: Integrity, since a chartered accountant shall not knowingly be associated with reports or certificates containing a materially false or misleading statement
options.A: Confidentiality, since the certificate discloses information about the client's asset register
options.C: Professional Behaviour only, with no violation of Integrity, since no law was directly broken
options.D: Objectivity, since the certificate did not involve any third-party influence

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Integrity, since a chartered accountant shall not knowingly be associated with reports or certificates containing a materially false or misleading statement

Integrity requires a chartered accountant to be straightforward and honest, and prohibits knowingly being associated with reports, returns, communications or other information containing a materially false or misleading statement. Knowingly certifying a cost figure significantly lower than the recorded figure, without basis, is a clear violation of Integrity.

question_html: What should CA Solkar conclude regarding point (i), the internally devised reporting framework lacking generally accepted characteristics?

options.A: The financial reporting framework does not appear to be acceptable, which is one of the two components of preconditions for an audit under SA 210; unless required by law or regulation, the firm should not accept the engagement on this basis alone
options.B: The framework is acceptable as long as the company discloses that it is internally devised, regardless of its characteristics
options.C: The framework's acceptability is irrelevant to preconditions for an audit, which relate only to management's cooperation
options.D: The framework should be accepted since financial reporting frameworks are entirely at the discretion of the entity being audited

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) The financial reporting framework does not appear to be acceptable, which is one of the two components of preconditions for an audit under SA 210; unless required by law or regulation, the firm should not accept the engagement on this basis alone

One of the two components of preconditions for an audit under SA 210 is the use by management of an acceptable financial reporting framework; a framework lacking generally accepted characteristics such as relevance, reliability, comparability, understandability and completeness would not be considered acceptable, and unless required by law, the auditor should not accept the engagement on that basis.

case_facts_html: Ambrish & Co. has been newly appointed as auditor of Wrenfield Publications Ltd. The engagement partner, CA Ambrish Talathi, is drafting the audit engagement letter to be sent to the Board of Directors. An article assistant, Kavya, raises three queries while assisting with the draft: (i) she asks whether the letter should describe the exact wording of the opinion the firm expects to issue at the end of the audit, since the audit has not yet begun; (ii) she asks whether the letter needs to separately state the responsibilities of both the auditor and of management, given that these are already understood informally; and (iii) she asks whether, once signed, the terms recorded in this year's engagement letter will automatically continue to apply, unchanged, to every future year's audit of Wrenfield Publications Ltd.
question_html: How should CA Talathi respond to Kavya's query (i), about describing the expected form and content of the auditor's report in the engagement letter?

options.D: The engagement letter should include reference to the expected form and content of the report to be issued, along with a statement that there may be circumstances in which the actual report may differ from its expected form and content
options.A: The engagement letter cannot refer to the form or content of the report at all, since the audit has not yet been performed
options.B: The engagement letter must state definitively and bindingly that only an unmodified opinion will be issued
options.C: The engagement letter should omit any reference to the report, and the report's form should be disclosed only after the audit is complete

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) The engagement letter should include reference to the expected form and content of the report to be issued, along with a statement that there may be circumstances in which the actual report may differ from its expected form and content

An audit engagement letter includes reference to the expected form and content of any reports to be issued by the auditor, together with a statement that there may be circumstances in which a report may differ from its expected form and content - the letter merely indicates the expected form, and if audit findings warrant a modified opinion, the auditor remains free to issue one.

subject: Auditing and Ethics
case_facts_html: Ambrish & Co. has been newly appointed as auditor of Wrenfield Publications Ltd. The engagement partner, CA Ambrish Talathi, is drafting the audit engagement letter to be sent to the Board of Directors. An article assistant, Kavya, raises three queries while assisting with the draft: (i) she asks whether the letter should describe the exact wording of the opinion the firm expects to issue at the end of the audit, since the audit has not yet begun; (ii) she asks whether the letter needs to separately state the responsibilities of both the auditor and of management, given that these are already understood informally; and (iii) she asks whether, once signed, the terms recorded in this year's engagement letter will automatically continue to apply, unchanged, to every future year's audit of Wrenfield Publications Ltd.
question_html: How should CA Talathi respond to Kavya's query (ii), about whether responsibilities need to be stated explicitly even though informally understood?

options.A: Yes, the engagement letter should explicitly state the responsibilities of both the auditor and of management, since a written record reduces the possibility of misunderstanding between the parties, regardless of any informal understanding
options.B: No, since an informal, undocumented understanding between the parties is legally equivalent to a written engagement letter
options.C: No, responsibilities need be stated only if the client specifically requests it in writing beforehand
options.D: Yes, but only the responsibilities of management need be stated; the auditor's own responsibilities are governed exclusively by SAs and need not appear in the letter

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Yes, the engagement letter should explicitly state the responsibilities of both the auditor and of management, since a written record reduces the possibility of misunderstanding between the parties, regardless of any informal understanding

It is important for both the auditor and client that each party is clear about the nature of the engagement, and it must be reduced to writing; the engagement letter should include the responsibilities of the auditor and the responsibilities of management, since issuing an engagement letter reduces the possibility of misunderstanding to a great extent, irrespective of any informal understanding.

case_facts_html: Vaidehi & Co. is the auditor of Thornbury Apparel Exports Ltd. Midway through the FY 2025-26 audit, the following events occur. Event 1: The company's export operations, which formed the basis for the original audit scope, are discontinued mid-year following a change in group strategy, and the company requests a corresponding, genuine revision of certain engagement terms to reflect the new, narrower scope of operations. Event 2: Separately, the audit team is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding a significant related-party receivable, and management, aware that this will likely result in a qualified opinion, requests that the engagement be changed to a review engagement instead. Event 3: After evaluating Event 2's request and declining to accede to it, the audit team finds that management refuses to permit them to continue the original audit engagement in any form.
question_html: How should Vaidehi & Co. treat the company's request in Event 1?

options.C: This may be considered a reasonable basis for a change, since it arises from a genuine change in circumstances affecting the entity's requirements (discontinuation of export operations), consistent with SA 210's guidance that such changes can justify revising the terms of engagement
options.A: This can never be considered reasonable, since SA 210 prohibits any change to engagement terms once fieldwork has commenced
options.B: This should be treated identically to Event 2's request, since both involve a change to engagement terms regardless of the underlying reason
options.D: This should be rejected outright, since only changes agreed before the engagement letter is signed can ever be considered under SA 210

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) This may be considered a reasonable basis for a change, since it arises from a genuine change in circumstances affecting the entity's requirements (discontinuation of export operations), consistent with SA 210's guidance that such changes can justify revising the terms of engagement

A change in circumstances that affects the entity's requirements may be considered a reasonable basis for requesting a change in the audit engagement; the genuine discontinuation of export operations, altering the scope of what needs to be audited, fits this description under SA 210.

case_facts_html: CA Ishwar Rathod is the engagement partner for the audit of Brightpath Consumer Goods Ltd. for FY 2025-26. Revenue from operations increased from ₹150 crore to ₹185 crore during the year, and net profit before tax increased from 6% to 11% of revenue, despite a two-month disruption in production caused by a labour strike at the company's largest manufacturing unit and a rejected insurance claim relating to inventory loss during the strike. CA Rathod's team notices a cluster of unusually large sales transactions recorded in the last week of the financial year, all routed through a single, newly onboarded distributor. When questioned, management provides sales invoices and delivery challans as support, and CA Rathod's audit senior proposes to close out the matter by relying solely on these documents and a standard management representation regarding the transactions' genuineness, without performing any further procedures such as confirming the transactions directly with the distributor or examining post-year-end credit notes and returns.
question_html: What is the primary concern with CA Rathod's audit senior proposing to close out the matter by relying solely on the invoices, delivery challans and a standard management representation?

options.A: This approach lacks professional skepticism, since the combination of a production disruption, a rejected insurance claim, and improved profitability alongside a cluster of unusual year-end transactions through a single new distributor calls for a more critical assessment of audit evidence and possibly additional procedures, not routine reliance on management-supplied documents alone
options.B: This approach is entirely appropriate, since invoices and delivery challans are always sufficient appropriate audit evidence regardless of surrounding circumstances
options.C: This approach is appropriate because management representations are, by themselves, always considered the most reliable form of audit evidence
options.D: This is not a matter for professional skepticism at all, since professional skepticism applies only to fraud specifically alleged by a whistleblower

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) This approach lacks professional skepticism, since the combination of a production disruption, a rejected insurance claim, and improved profitability alongside a cluster of unusual year-end transactions through a single new distributor calls for a more critical assessment of audit evidence and possibly additional procedures, not routine reliance on management-supplied documents alone

Maintaining professional skepticism throughout the audit is necessary to reduce the risk of overlooking unusual circumstances and using inappropriate assumptions in determining the nature, timing and extent of audit procedures; the unusual profitability trend despite the strike, combined with the year-end transaction cluster through a new distributor, are unusual circumstances calling for a critical assessment of evidence, not routine closure of the matter.

case_facts_html: SRV & Co., Chartered Accountants, are statutory auditors of Meridian Infra Holdings Ltd., a listed company. During the audit for FY 2025-26, the Engagement Partner, CA Vikramjit Oswal, becomes aware of the following: (i) the spouse of a senior member of the engagement team has recently acquired a substantial shareholding in Meridian Infra Holdings Ltd.; (ii) the firm has, during the same year, provided the client with consultancy services relating to implementation of a new enterprise risk management framework; and (iii) one of the firm's partners has separately been offered, and is considering accepting, a seat on the advisory council of a group entity promoted by the same persons who control Meridian Infra Holdings Ltd. Some of CA Oswal's fellow partners argue that, given the significance of the client's fees to the firm, these matters should not be allowed to jeopardise the relationship.
question_html: Which threats to independence are raised by matters (i), (ii) and (iii) respectively?

options.C: (i) is a self-interest threat (financial interest held by a team member's spouse), (ii) is a self-review threat (non-audit consultancy services that may need to be evaluated as part of the audit), and (iii) is a familiarity threat (a partner's prospective close association with a group entity controlled by the same persons)
options.A: All three matters represent the same single threat category (advocacy threat) and should be assessed identically
options.B: (i) is an intimidation threat, (ii) is an advocacy threat, and (iii) has no bearing on independence whatsoever
options.D: None of the three matters raise any threat to independence, since none involve a direct financial interest held personally by CA Oswal

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) (i) is a self-interest threat (financial interest held by a team member's spouse), (ii) is a self-review threat (non-audit consultancy services that may need to be evaluated as part of the audit), and (iii) is a familiarity threat (a partner's prospective close association with a group entity controlled by the same persons)

A team member's spouse holding shares in the client creates a self-interest threat; the firm's provision of ERM consultancy services to the same client creates a self-review threat, since the audit may need to evaluate matters arising from that consultancy; and a partner's prospective advisory role with a group entity controlled by the client's controlling persons creates a familiarity threat arising from a close, ongoing association.

question_html: Is the view of CA Oswal's fellow partners - that the matters should not be allowed to jeopardise the relationship given the significance of the client's fees - consistent with SA 220 and the fundamental principles?

options.A: No, undue dependence on a client's fees is itself a self-interest threat, and allowing fee significance to override the evaluation of independence threats would compound rather than resolve the problem; the Engagement Partner is duty-bound to evaluate the identified threats and take appropriate corrective action (such as disposal of the financial interest, removal of affected personnel, discontinuation of conflicting services, or withdrawal) regardless of fee considerations
options.B: Yes, the significance of a client's fees to the firm is, by itself, an acceptable safeguard against any threat to independence under SA 220
options.C: Yes, provided the firm documents the partners' view in the engagement file, no further action is required regardless of the threats identified
options.D: No response is needed, since SA 220 applies only to non-listed clients and Meridian Infra Holdings Ltd. is listed

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) No, undue dependence on a client's fees is itself a self-interest threat, and allowing fee significance to override the evaluation of independence threats would compound rather than resolve the problem; the Engagement Partner is duty-bound to evaluate the identified threats and take appropriate corrective action (such as disposal of the financial interest, removal of affected personnel, discontinuation of conflicting services, or withdrawal) regardless of fee considerations

Undue dependence on a client's fees is itself listed as an example of a self-interest threat; allowing fee significance to override an honest evaluation of independence threats would itself be a further threat to independence. Under SA 220, if identified threats cannot be eliminated or reduced to an acceptable level through safeguards, the firm must either eliminate the underlying cause or withdraw from the engagement, as permitted by law - failure to do so would amount to non-compliance with SA 220.

case_facts_html: Kalpavriksh & Co., a firm of Chartered Accountants, is offered appointment as auditor of Everline Wellness Products Ltd., a prospective new client. CA Ridhima, one of the partners, is leading the discussions with the company's officers and discovers that the company's newly appointed CFO, Mr. Yohan, was her senior at the same coaching institute many years ago, though they have had no contact since. During preliminary discussions, it emerges that the company wants the audit firm's partners to be present alongside company representatives at investor roadshows to lend credibility to the company's growth projections. The firm writes to the previous auditor, Kestrel & Associates, seeking their views on any professional reasons for not accepting the engagement, but Kestrel & Associates does not respond despite two reminders. Separately, during due diligence, Kalpavriksh & Co. discovers that the company recently acquired a controlling stake in another entity, triggering a statutory requirement for consolidated financial statements, but the firm does not think it necessary to bring this to the company's attention at this stage. The company additionally proposes that the firm also take up a separate contract to manage the company's payroll processing function going forward.
question_html: What type of threat to independence would arise if Kalpavriksh & Co.'s partners agree to be visibly present alongside company representatives at investor roadshows to lend credibility to growth projections?

options.B: Advocacy threat, since the firm would be perceived as promoting the client's growth projections to investors, potentially compromising perceived objectivity
options.A: Self-review threat, since roadshow participation would require reviewing the firm's own prior audit conclusions
options.C: Intimidation threat, since investors could pressure the firm regarding future audit opinions
options.D: No threat at all, since attending investor events is a routine marketing activity unconnected to audit independence

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Advocacy threat, since the firm would be perceived as promoting the client's growth projections to investors, potentially compromising perceived objectivity

Advocacy threats occur when the auditor promotes, or is perceived to promote, a client's opinion (here, its growth projections) to a point where people may believe objectivity is compromised; visible participation alongside the client at investor roadshows to lend credibility is a clear example of such a threat.
